The danger that we face is not inherently military; it’s not armies in the conventional sense. It is above all ideological. As long as millions of people are committed fanatically to doctrines that are ultimately mad and that follow in the tradition of the totalitarian madnesses of Europe in the twentieth century, the danger persists. I maintain that the struggle we are involved in is, or ought to be, ultimately a war of ideas.

Paul Berman (2003)

The Choice That Started a War  

Paris was a prince of Troy, born to King Priam and Queen Hecuba. 
Before his birth, his mother had a prophetic dream, which a seer interpreted to mean that the baby would cause the total destruction of the city. To save Troy, his parents reluctantly ordered him to be exposed on Mount Ida. 

However, a shepherd found the infant, saved him, and raised him as his own son. Paris grew up tending flocks, completely unaware of his royal heritage. 

His life changed when Eris, the goddess of discord, threw a golden apple inscribed with the words "To the Fairest" into a divine banquet. 

Three powerful goddesses
- Hera, Athena, and Aphrodite - all claimed it. 

Zeus refused to judge the contest himself and instead appointed Paris to make the final decision.

The goddesses descended to Mount Ida and attempted to bribe him

Hera offered him vast political power, promising to make him emperor of Europe and Asia

Athena offered him absolute wisdom and supreme mastery in military combat

Aphrodite offered him the love of Helen of Sparta, renowned as the most beautiful mortal woman in the world.

Paris awarded the golden apple to Aphrodite

This choice earned him the permanent hatred of Hera and Athena, sealing the tragic fate of Troy.

Shortly after, Paris was rediscovered by his royal family and welcomed back as a prince of Troy. 

He then sailed on a diplomatic mission to Sparta, where, with Aphrodite's magical help, he seduced and abducted Helen. 

Because Helen was already married to King Menelaus of Sparta, her abduction triggered a massive alliance of Greek kings. 

They launched a massive fleet to besiege Troy, igniting the legendary Trojan War, which raged for 10 grueling years before Troy was finally destroyed.

#Tehran appears to believe that a political window is opening in Washington. With the U.S. midterm elections approaching and President Trump facing strong incentives to bring down oil prices, Iran sees an opportunity to test whether economic and political pressure can translate into American flexibility.

But Tehran’s position should not be mistaken for a fundamental strategic retreat. At its core, Iran is still insisting on its key red lines and, in important respects, seeking a return to the framework established in the earlier memorandum of understanding — a framework the Trump administration has since moved away from.

That makes the central question for Washington not simply whether it should accept or reject Iran’s latest proposal. The more consequential question is: What happens the day after Washington says no?

Iranian leaders are also reading the American political calendar. They understand that a major escalation before the midterms could impose significant political and economic costs on the administration, particularly through higher oil and gasoline prices. Trump himself has publicly acknowledged the connection between the Iran conflict, energy prices and the midterm timetable.

If Tehran concludes that Washington wants to avoid a broader confrontation before November, it may decide that escalation,  rather than compromise, offers the better path to leverage. The question then becomes whether Iran would move beyond absorbing the economic pressure of the U.S. blockade and take new steps to impose costs on Washington and the global economy, particularly around maritime traffic and energy flows.

The Strait of Hormuz has already become one of Tehran’s principal sources of leverage. Recent negotiations have centered precisely on the tradeoff between reopening the strait and easing the U.S. blockade.

So the administration should evaluate the Iranian proposal against two scenarios, not one. The first is the cost and strategic consequence of accepting a deal that largely revives the previous framework. The second is the likely Iranian response if Washington rejects it.

The real policy question is therefore not only whether Iran’s offer is acceptable. It is whether Washington has a credible strategy for what comes next if it is not.

text:
Long before reclamation pushed Manila Bay far from Calle Real, there stood a Parañaque home so lavish that stories about it bordered on the unbelievable.

It had a grand European-inspired façade, sprawling grounds for receptions, its own swimming pool and a sweeping view of Manila Bay. At a time when Parañaque still had beachfront estates, the Don Adolfo Garcia Residence was reportedly the kind of place where Manila’s elite gathered for spectacular parties.

Accounts about the Garcia family home even described it as being second only to Malacañang Palace in opulence.

And incredibly, the house is still standing.

The Parañaque City Tourism Office recently drew attention to the historic residence at 517 Calle Real, describing its architecture as having characteristics of a French château.

According to research cited by the tourism office and attributed to Garcia family descendants, the residence was designed by Andrés Luna de San Pedro, architect and son of Filipino master painter Juan Luna.

Old photographs and family accounts offer a glimpse of just how extraordinary the property once was. The enormous residence had spaces capable of accommodating large receptions and a swimming pool—a remarkable luxury in prewar Manila. The Garcia-Llamas family was among the country’s wealthy Spanish-mestizo clans, and its Parañaque beach home became synonymous with their privileged world.

The family also produced an important Filipino artist.

Don Adolfo’s son Antonio Garcia Llamas became one of the best-known portrait painters of postwar Philippine high society. He studied in Spain and Italy, later taught at the University of Santo Tomas and painted prominent Filipinos. A portrait he made of Ramon Magsaysay is part of the Malacañang collection.

But war dramatically changed the Garcia mansion’s story.

According to an account involving Garcia-Llamas family history, Don Adolfo feared that Japanese forces would eventually take over the property. Toward the end of World War II, he reportedly sold the mansion for a staggering ₱300,000.

There was one devastating catch: he was paid in Japanese-issued currency—the notorious “Mickey Mouse money” that became virtually worthless with Japan’s defeat.

The Parañaque City Tourism Office says the mansion itself would become part of the liberation story. On February 3, 1945, it served as a headquarters for American forces during operations to free Parañaque from Japanese occupation.

After the war, according to the tourism office, the residence passed through the hands of prominent political families. Cebu senator Manuel C. Briones first acquired it, followed later by former Agusan del Sur representative and governor Democrito O. Plaza.

Today, the mansion no longer looks out directly onto the beach that helped make it legendary. Decades of development and coastal reclamation radically transformed this part of Parañaque.

Yet the old house survives—a physical reminder that behind the traffic, concrete and rapidly changing skyline of modern Metro Manila are remnants of an entirely different city.

Perhaps that is what makes the Don Adolfo Garcia Residence remarkable.

A house that once entertained Manila’s elite, witnessed war, reportedly became an American military headquarters, survived the disappearance of the beach outside its doors and outlived the fortune and society that created it is still there.

And for many Filipinos passing through Parañaque today, one of the grandest houses of prewar Manila has been hiding in plain sight.

(✍️:Top Dagohoy)

text:
I think “Reopen” is an interesting term and doing a lot of hard work to make this sound like a good offer, when it isn’t. 

Iran has consistently said it will "open" Hormuz in any deal, but unfortunately it is not under any pre-war interpretation of the term. 

They have said since the MoU this means opening under Iranian arrangements developed with Oman, where Iran will establish control over (at least in bound) traffic. The terms of reopening therefore will legitimise Iranian control and immediately end the dark shuttle transits via  Oman coastal waters that have been so key to getting much needed volumes of oil to market, not least at a time when Red Sea oil exports are heavily disrupted. 

This offer is consistent with Iranian objectives for sometime - open Hormuz on their terms (which gives them considerable, lasting control), whilst immediately ending the dark transit route. Meanwhile they get access to market for their oil.  

Of course they would want this. Not sure the US, its allies or the markets would be happy with the implications when the dust settles. Saudi Arabia and the GCC may be prepared to accept this right now, out of fatigue and frustration with a lack of deliverable plan from the US to end the conflict. And I agree, China have been explicit in their support of a return to the MoU principles

So this offer would give Iran several “wins “ but in return, the strait would not open the strait  on any pre-war model of what that means. In fact Iranian “control” of the strait, legitimised in an initial deal, would give them additional leverage for any talks on a “lasting settlement” on nuclear etc

All gain, no pain for Iran. Could the US really accept that? It’s possible but not without some considerable costs to US geopolitical power and prestige.

👀🏁 Shane McElrath revealed that this actually ISN’T the first time he and Beta have seriously talked about working together.

A couple years ago, Beta made him what he described as a really good offer. 💰🔥

There was just one problem:

📍 He would have had to move to California.

For Shane and his family, that was enough to kill the deal at the time. Between the move, higher expenses and California taxes, he said the money suddenly didn’t make nearly as much sense. 💸🏠

So they passed.

Fast-forward a couple years and the situation looks completely different. 🔄👀

Beta has had more time to develop the 450, the Supercross program has matured, and when McElrath finally went out to test the bike this time, he came away impressed almost immediately. 🏍️🔧🔥

Now the timing actually works.

✅ Better-developed bike
✅ Factory backing
✅ Clear Supercross focus
✅ A deal that works for Shane’s life
✅ No requirement that forced the family into a move that didn’t make sense

Sometimes a deal isn’t necessarily wrong.

It’s just wrong at that moment.

A couple years later, McElrath and Beta finally found the version that worked for both sides. 🤝🔥

The Lead
Xi Visit Shows the Potential for a New Outlook in Thinking

by Stewart Battle (EIRNS) — Sep. 24, 2026

During his joint press conference at the White House with President Donald Trump on Sep. 24, Chinese President Xi Jinping gave the following formulation: While cooperation between the U.S. and China “may not solve every problem in the world,” without it, “it would be hard to solve many of the world’s problems.” This truthful remark was important for President Trump to hear, who, despite presiding over a breathtaking and glamorous state visit honoring the Chinese leader, was struggling to understand the significance the event itself held.

The visit began with the almost unprecedented greeting of President Xi by Trump and First Lady Melania at Andrews Air Force Base, marking the first time a sitting U.S. President greeted a visiting head of state at the airport in over 60 years. The pair then held a joint ceremony, presided over a military troop review in the Rose Garden, held high-level talks in the Oval Office, and enjoyed a lavish state dinner at the White House.

But this is the same Donald Trump who, two days earlier during his remarks to the UN General Assembly, had threatened to “annihilate” Iran, dismissed the very concept of cooperation in favor of the law of the jungle, and expressed the notion of “to the winner, the spoils,” as could be seen in the case of Venezuela.

Xi wrote in a statement released on the eve of his visit: “China and the United States should be partners, not rivals”—the very phrase and concept which Xi and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi had just agreed to during their meeting at the BRICS Summit. “The great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and making America great again can go hand in hand,” Xi added, and later proclaimed at the White House that “the Thucydides trap can be overcome.” Trump, for his part, said that he and Xi had “forged a friendship… built on mutual respect and the vital interests of our people.” He referenced the U.S.-China alliance to defeat fascism during World War II, and noted: “Just as our people worked together to win that war, President Xi and I will continue working together to forge a better future for both of our nations.”

As far as it goes, the visit exemplifies the potential collaboration between the two countries—arguably one of the most consequential relationships in the world today. However, while Xi’s actions have followed his words, Trump’s actions have not yet followed his.

Led by London, European and Western nations are pledging more and more support to Ukraine in a dangerous escalation toward all-out war with Russia. And the U.S. itself recently passed the Lindsey Graham Sanctions Act that will punish other nations for even trading with Russia. In addition, a dangerous rearmament is ongoing throughout Europe that is setting the stage for new and future conflicts. The UK is now joining in the Trump administration’s initiative of weaponizing space, and is forming a special squadron in the Royal Air Force for the purposes of “disrupting, degrading, and denying enemy activity… in space.” “This century will depend on control of space,” British Defense Minister Wes Streeting said.

At the same time, the British have their strategic allies in the U.S. who are hell-bent on stopping any cooperation. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer said, at a Sep. 23 press conference alongside Democratic Senators Elizabeth Warren, Andy Kim and Elissa Slotkin: “Trump is handing China the technology it needs to win the AI race.” All four senators demanded Trump stop further advanced semiconductor exports to China, and insisted China be held accountable for assisting Iran in the current war. Slotkin said watching Trump welcome Xi to the White House “is really difficult.”

This is not the view of China, nor of the growing portion of the world which is increasingly rejecting the failed unipolar model in favor of a new global architecture. As Helga Zepp-LaRouche put it in her weekly webcast on Sep. 23, there is a “whole group of nations rallying around a new principle, and that is the idea of partnership, of diplomacy, of coexistence, of the idea that the new name for peace is development, and to rule out war as a means of conflict resolution by basically saying that only diplomacy and negotiations are legitimate.” And between the approach of the defenders of the unipolar order, she remarked, “there seems to be a widening gap.”

It is now an urgent necessity to put this perspective on the table, and to mobilize awareness within the nations of the West that such an alternative option exists. The UN General Assembly this week offers an excellent opportunity in that regard. Tune in to Friday’s meeting of the International Peace Coalition, which will take up these questions in more depth. https://t.co/Hvz4Mi5xLE
